items.title: Meta Job Listing Explicitly References Its Humanoid Robot Hardware
items.summary: A Meta job listing for a Mechanical Design Engineer explicitly references work on humanoid robot hardware after its initial release. The role focuses on maintaining and improving the physical machines through addressing mechanical failures and assembly improvements. Responsibilities include investigating component issues, implementing design changes, and working with fabrication teams to resolve build problems. The position requires experience in manufacturing and sustaining engineering, involving components like motors and actuators. This posting details the engineering work required to support the development and production of Meta's humanoid robot hardware.

items.title: Agility CEO Peggy Johnson Joins Project Meridian, Bringing Humanoid Logistics Expertise to Defense Study
items.summary: Agility Robotics CEO Peggy Johnson will join Project Meridian, a MITRE-led study on future warfare, as an individual consultant. She will contribute expertise from commercial humanoid deployments to discussions about military logistics and operational support. Johnson suggests humanoids can assist service personnel by handling demanding, repetitive logistics tasks to improve supply chains. Project Meridian aims to develop recommendations over a long-term horizon for future warfighting capabilities. This participation places commercial humanoid experience within a strategic defense planning context.

Johnson intends to contribute insights derived from commercial humanoid deployments to discussions regarding military logistics and operational support. This participation bridges commercial humanoid innovation with strategic defense planning frameworks. The integration of physical automation into defense strategy warrants continued observation from the technology sector.

items.title: ROS Discourse General: University of Waterloo user study on understanding CMake changes
items.summary: A user study is being conducted by a University of Waterloo Ph.D. candidate to understand how developers perceive changes to CMake build specifications. The study evaluates a new approach designed to help users identify the impact of these modifications on the resulting build configuration. Participation is open to individuals aged 18–64 with any experience in CMake, programming, or code review. The study is entirely online, lasts about one hour, and will not collect participants' names. The research has received clearance from the University of Waterloo Research Ethics Board.
items.audio_script:
From Planet ROS, "ROS Discourse General: University of Waterloo user study on understanding CMake changes". This report details a user study conducted by a University of Waterloo Ph.D. candidate to understand how developers perceive changes to CMake build specifications. The research evaluates a new approach designed to help users identify the impact of these modifications on the resulting build configuration. The study involved participants aged eighteen to sixty-four with any experience in CMake, programming, or code review. The research was conducted entirely online over a duration of approximately one hour and received clearance from the University of Waterloo Research Ethics Board.

The methodology involved assessing developer perception regarding modifications to CMake build specifications using the new approach to gauge the impact visibility. Participants engaged with the study to evaluate how effectively the proposed method assists in understanding the consequences of these build specification changes. The research aimed to gather empirical data on the efficacy of this new framework for build configuration comprehension.

This research provides insight into developer workflows for managing complex build systems. Future developments in build tooling may utilize these findings to improve developer experience across the technology sector.
